cor-cor-slope-covariance.title: Covariance of the slopes under normal regressors
cor-cor-slope-covariance.title_html: Covariance of the slopes under normal regressors
cor-cor-slope-covariance.html: Let the rows (Xi⊤,Yi) be independent draws from a (k+1)-variate normal distribution with ΣXX positive definite and conditional variance σ2=Var(Y∣X), and let β^ be the least squares slopes from a fit with an intercept. If n≥k+3, E(β^)=β,Cov(β^)=σ2n−k−2ΣXX−1.

def-cor-pure-error.title: Pure error and lack of fit
def-cor-pure-error.title_html: Pure error and lack of fit
def-cor-pure-error.html:
With MZ the projection onto C(Z), the pure error and lack-of-fit sums of squares are SSPE=‖(I−MZ)y‖2=∑i=1c∑j=1ni(yij−y¯i)2,SSLF=‖(MZ−M)y‖2=∑i=1cni(y¯i−y^i)2,{#eq-cor-sspe}

with n−c and c−r degrees of freedom, where y^i=xi⊤β^ is the common fitted value of group i and r=rank(X).

def-cor-random-regressors.title: Normal linear model with random regressors
def-cor-random-regressors.title_html: Normal linear model with random regressors
def-cor-random-regressors.html: Let X be a random n×p matrix and Y a random n-vector. They follow the normal linear model with random regressors if rank(X)=p with probability one and, conditionally on X, Y∣X ∼ Nn(Xβ,σ2In) for constants β∈Rp and σ2>0. Equivalently, Y=Xβ+ε with ε∼Nn(0,σ2In) independent of X.

def-cor-sample-partial.title: Sample partial correlation
def-cor-sample-partial.html: Let y,x∈Rn, let Z be an n×q matrix, and let D=[1,Z] have rank q+1<n. With MD the projection onto C(D), put y~=(I−MD)y and x~=(I−MD)x, and suppose both are nonzero. The sample partial correlation of y and x given Z is ryx⋅Z=y~⊤x~‖y~‖‖x~‖.

def-cor-wishart.title: Wishart distribution
def-cor-wishart.html: Let the rows of the m×k matrix Z be independent Nk(0,Σ) vectors. The law of W=Z⊤Z=∑i=1mzizi⊤ is the Wishart distribution Wk(m,Σ) with m degrees of freedom. For k=1, W1(m,σ2) is the law of σ2χ2(m).

eq-cor-blup.html: y^0=x0⊤β~+v0⊤V−1(Y−Xβ~),

eq-cor-fisher-z.html: z=tanh−1⁡r=12log⁡1+r1−r,ζ=tanh−1⁡ρ.

eq-cor-lof-noncentrality.html: γ=‖(I−M)θ‖2σ2=1σ2∑i=1cni(μi−μ~i)2,

eq-cor-prediction-error.html: E(Y0−Y^0)2=σ2(1+1n)n−2n−k−2.

eq-cor-r-cdf.html: Pr(r≤c)=E[Pr{t(n−2,δV)≤cn−2/1−c2}].

eq-cor-r2-mixture.html: Pr(R2≤c)=E[Pr{F(k,n−k−1,λV)≤(n−k−1)ck(1−c)}].

eq-cor-r2-plugin.html: R2=sXY⊤SXX−1sXYsY2,

eq-cor-random-noncentrality.html: γ(X)=(Λ⊤β−d)⊤[Λ⊤(X⊤X)−1Λ]−1(Λ⊤β−d)σ2.

eq-cor-signal-noise.html: σ2=σY2(1−ρY⋅X2),β⊤ΣXXβ=σY2ρY⋅X2,soβ⊤ΣXXβσ2=ρY⋅X21−ρY⋅X2.

eq-cor-slope-variance.html: Var(β^1)=σ2σX2(n−3).

eq-cor-smoother-statistic.html: T=‖Sε^‖2‖ε^‖2.

eq-cor-sspe.html: SSPE=‖(I−MZ)y‖2=∑i=1c∑j=1ni(yij−y¯i)2,SSLF=‖(MZ−M)y‖2=∑i=1cni(y¯i−y^i)2,

eq-cor-z-interval.html: tanh⁡(z−zα/2n−3) ≤ ρ ≤ tanh⁡(z+zα/2n−3),

exm-cor-conditional-power.title: How much power has this design?
exm-cor-conditional-power.title_html: How much power has this design?
exm-cor-conditional-power.html: Take n=12, σ=σX=1 and slope 0.6. The test of a zero slope at level 0.05 has conditional power between 0.321 and 0.518 for the middle half of the designs, with median 0.414 (panel (c) of Figure 14.1.1). The unconditional power, the average over designs, is 0.425; a direct simulation of the whole procedure gives 0.426. Plugging in the average design, Sxx=n−1, gives 0.436, which overstates the power a study should expect.

exm-cor-lof-power.title: Two departures, five tests
exm-cor-lof-power.html:
Take n=50 equally spaced values of x in (0,1), a straight-line working model, standard normal errors, and five tests at level 0.05: adding x2; RESET with squared and cubed fitted values; a cubic spline with knots at 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75; near replicates formed by 10 clusters of 5 neighbouring values; and the smoother statistic @eq-cor-smoother-statistic with Gaussian kernel weights of bandwidth 0.06, its critical value simulated from 50000 null residual vectors. Over 4000 samples from the straight line, the rejection rates are 0.050, 0.054, 0.054, 0.052 and 0.054: all five tests are exact.

Against smooth curvature, a mean of 1+2x+6(x−0.5)2, the powers are 0.874 for the quadratic term, 0.786 for RESET (which here is the cubic polynomial test), 0.606 for the spline, 0.422 for near replicates and 0.723 for the smoother. Against a narrow bump of height 2.5 near x=0.8, the order is reversed: the smoother has power 0.622, the spline 0.501, near replicates 0.459, RESET 0.227, and the quadratic term 0.029, below the level: the bump is nearly orthogonal to x2 after the line is removed, so it inflates the denominator of that test without feeding its numerator. Figure 14.7.1 shows the power curves.

exm-cor-partial-simulation.title: Twelve cases, two skewed conditioning variables
exm-cor-partial-simulation.title_html: Twelve cases, two skewed conditioning variables
exm-cor-partial-simulation.html: Take n=12, q=2 conditioning variables drawn as squares of exponential variables, which are very skewed, a pair whose conditional means depend linearly on them, and conditional correlation ρ=0.6. Over 100000 samples, the 10%, 50% and 90% points of the sample partial correlation are 0.257, 0.624 and 0.834. For ordinary correlations from n−q=10 normal pairs they are 0.256, 0.625 and 0.835. A two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test finds no difference between the two sets of simulated values (p-value 0.09).

exm-cor-r2-bias.title: How biased is R-squared?
exm-cor-r2-bias.html: With n=25, k=4 and 100000 simulated samples, the averages of R2 are 0.1669, 0.4026 and 0.6500 for ρ2=0, 0.3 and 0.6, against exact values 0.1667, 0.4026 and 0.6498. The exact values come from the formula E(R2)=1−n−k−1n−1(1−ρ2)2F1(1,1;n+12;ρ2), which follows from Fisher’s (1928) distribution of R2 (see Olkin and Pratt 1958), where 2F1 is the hypergeometric function; it can also be computed from @eq-cor-r2-mixture. The bias shrinks as ρ2 grows. The adjusted R2 of @eq-ss-adjusted-r2 averages 0.0003, 0.2831 and 0.5800: unbiased under the null (@prp-ss-adjusted-r2(e)), but biased downwards when ρ2>0. Neither is unbiased everywhere. The standard deviations of R2 are 0.104, 0.146 and 0.118: with 25 cases, a single R2 says little about ρ2.

exm-cor-rand-prediction.title: Predicting doctor visits
exm-cor-rand-prediction.html: The RAND Health Insurance Experiment records, for 20190 person-years, the number of outpatient visits and characteristics of the insurance plan and of the person. Treat these rows as the population, and predict log⁡(1+visits) linearly from 6 of the characteristics (coinsurance rate, deductible and participation-incentive terms, maximum expenditure, physical limitation and a chronic-disease index). The population projection has mean squared error 0.6330 and explains a fraction 0.094 of the variance. Draw training samples of 40 rows, fit by least squares, and evaluate each fit exactly on the whole population. Over 4000 training samples the average in-sample error is 0.5182 and the average error on new cases is 0.8201, against normal-theory values 0.5223 and 0.7705 from @prp-cor-optimism(b). The normal-theory value understates the error on new cases: the regressors are far from normal (two are indicators, one skewed), the linear predictor need not be the conditional mean, and the error variance need not be constant; the formula assumes none of this. It is a first guide to the optimism, not a substitute for checking it.

exm-cor-skewed-design.title: Skewed regressors
exm-cor-skewed-design.html: Take n=10 cases with an intercept and two regressors drawn afresh for every sample, one exponential and one lognormal, and E(Y)=1+0⋅x1+0.5x2. The t test of β1=0 at level 0.05 uses the t(7) quantile. Over 100000 samples with standard normal errors independent of the regressors, the test rejects in a proportion 0.0508 of them, as @thm-cor-conditional requires; panel (b) of Figure 14.1.1 shows the simulated statistics against the t(7) density. If instead the error of each case is multiplied by its own value of x1, so that the spread depends on the regressor, the same test rejects in a proportion 0.2798. The conditional model no longer holds, and nothing in the theorem protects the test.

exm-cor-slope-simulation.title: A heavy-tailed slope
exm-cor-slope-simulation.html: With n=12, σX=2, σ=1 and slope 0.5, the variance of the slope over 100000 simulated samples, each with its own design, is 0.02751, against 0.02778 from @eq-cor-slope-variance and 0.02273 from the naive guess. The excess kurtosis of the simulated slopes is 0.85, close to the value 0.86 of the t(11) distribution. Panel (a) of Figure 14.1.1 shows the tails on a logarithmic scale. The scaled t(11) density follows the simulated slopes, and the normal density with the same variance falls away too fast.

exm-cor-stackloss-full.title: Is the three-variable model adequate?
exm-cor-stackloss-full.html: Return to the stack loss data with air flow, water temperature and acid concentration, n=21 and r=4. Ward clustering of the standardized rows into 8 clusters and testing X against [X,D] gives F=1.43 on 7 and 10 degrees of freedom (p-value 0.292). Adding the squares of the three regressors gives F=1.92 on 3 and 14 (p-value 0.172). The rainbow test with the 11 cases of smallest leverage as the central subset gives F=1.04 on 10 and 7 (p-value 0.497), and RESET gives F=1.17 on 2 and 15 (p-value 0.336). None of the tests finds lack of fit. The strong lack of fit of the line in air flow alone (@exm-cor-stackloss-lof) was the omitted water temperature, which varies within the groups of equal air flow. With 21 cases none of these tests is powerful, and a few unusual days deserve the scrutiny of Chapter 20.

exm-cor-stackloss-lof.title: Stack loss and air flow
exm-cor-stackloss-lof.html:
Brownlee’s stack loss data record n=21 days of operation of a plant that oxidizes ammonia. Air flow, the rate of operation, takes only c=7 distinct values, so a straight-line regression of stack loss on air flow can be tested for lack of fit with 14 degrees of freedom for pure error. The line has intercept −44.13 and slope 1.020, and R2=0.846. Its residual sum of squares 319.12 splits into SSPE=96.53 and SSLF=222.58 on 5 degrees of freedom. The mean squares are 44.52 and 6.90, so F=6.46 with p-value 0.0026; the 5% point of F(5,14) is 2.96. The residual mean square of the line, 16.80, is more than twice the pure-error estimate of σ2.

Figure 14.6.1 shows why. The group means do not lie on any smooth curve: the single day at air flow 70 has stack loss 15.0, below the mean 20.6 of the five days at air flow 62. A parabola does not help, with F=7.22 on 4 and 14 degrees of freedom (p-value 0.0023). The mean of stack loss is not a function of air flow alone, which points to the other operating variables, taken up in @exm-cor-stackloss-full.

exm-cor-states-correlation.title: Poverty and graduation
exm-cor-states-correlation.html: Across the 50 states, the correlation between the poverty rate and the high-school graduation rate is r=−0.7613. Its t statistic for ρ=0 is −8.13 on 48 degrees of freedom, far out in the tail. The Fisher interval @eq-cor-z-interval is (−0.858,−0.613) and the exact interval is (−0.855,−0.609), almost the same, and both are noticeably asymmetric about r.

exm-cor-states-partial.title: Violent crime and urbanization
exm-cor-states-partial.html: Across the 50 states, the violent crime rate and the urbanization rate have correlation 0.345. Given the percentage of single-parent households and the poverty rate (q=2), their partial correlation is r=0.1863. In the regression of violent crime on the three variables and an intercept, the coefficient of urbanization is 1.388 with t=1.286 on 46 degrees of freedom (p-value 0.2049), and indeed 46r/1−r2=1.286. With n−q=48, the Fisher interval for ρyx⋅Z is (−0.103,0.447) and the exact interval is (−0.103,0.443). Much of the marginal association is shared with single parenthood and poverty, and what remains is compatible with none.

exm-cor-states-r2.title: Violent crime in the states
exm-cor-states-r2.html: For the 50 states in 2009, regress the violent crime rate on the high-school graduation rate, the poverty rate, the percentage of single-parent households, the percentage of white residents and the urbanization rate. Then R2=0.4607, the adjusted value is 0.3994, and F=7.52 on 5 and 44 degrees of freedom, with p-value 3.6×10−5. Read with random regressors, the 95% interval for ρ2 is (0.175,0.610). The interval is wide: five regressors and fifty cases leave much room for chance. It also treats the states as a random sample, which they are not; it describes hypothetical replications of a process generating rows like these, and here, as in @exm-cor-states-correlation, no more can be claimed.

exr-cor-adaptive-design.title: B2
exr-cor-adaptive-design.html: Suppose a pilot sample is used to choose the regressor values of the main study, so that the distribution of X in the main study depends on β. Assume that, given X, the main-study responses follow the normal linear model with errors independent of the pilot. Show that the t test of @thm-cor-conditional(a), computed from the main study alone, still has exact size. Why is the design no longer ancillary, and what information about β does the t test ignore?

exr-cor-ar1-forecast.title: B2
exr-cor-ar1-forecast.html: Let the errors of a regression follow a stationary autoregression, et=ϕet−1+ut, |ϕ|<1, with white noise ut, so that Cov(es,et)∝ϕ|s−t|. Observe t=1,…,n and predict yn+1=xn+1⊤β+en+1. Show that V−1v0=ϕen, the last standard basis vector scaled by ϕ, and hence that the BLUP is xn+1⊤β~+ϕ(yn−xn⊤β~).

exr-cor-average-variance-interval.title: C1
exr-cor-average-variance-interval.html: In the setting of @prp-cor-slope-unconditional, with σ known, consider the interval β^1±1.96σ/(n−1)σX2, which uses the average design instead of the observed one. Show that its coverage given the design is 2Φ(1.96V/(n−1))−1 with V∼χ2(n−1), and that its unconditional coverage is below 0.95. Which designs make it badly wrong, and in which direction?

exr-cor-collider.title: C1
exr-cor-collider.html: Let X and Y be independent N(0,1) and C=X+Y+U with U∼N(0,1) independent of both. Compute ρXY⋅C. With n=200 cases, what does the t test of the coefficient of X in the regression of Y on C and X tend to conclude? Is the conclusion about the relation between X and Y wrong, or is the question wrong?

exr-cor-fitted-random.title: B1
exr-cor-fitted-random.html: In the setting of @prp-cor-slope-unconditional, let x0 be a fixed value and μ^0=β^0+β^1x0 the fitted mean there. Show that Var(μ^0)=σ2[1n+(x0−μX)2+σX2/nσX2(n−3)]. Hint: X¯ and Sxx are independent.

exr-cor-hat-rows.title: B3
exr-cor-hat-rows.html: Show that rows i and j of M are equal iff rows i and j of X are equal. So replicates can be read off the hat matrix.

exr-cor-linearized.title: B1
exr-cor-linearized.html: For any predictor g(X) with 0<Varg<∞, let g~=EY+b(g−Eg) with b=Cov(Y,g)/Varg. Show that g~ predicts at least as well as g and that E(Y−g~)2=Var(Y)(1−corr(Y,g)2). Conclude that among such linearized predictors, a higher squared correlation with Y means a smaller mean squared error, and that @eq-cor-correlation-ratio identifies the best of them.

exr-cor-lof-below-level.title: B3
exr-cor-lof-below-level.html: In @prp-cor-augmented-test, suppose θ=Xβ+δ with δ≠0 orthogonal to C(Z). Show that the power of the test is strictly less than its size.

exr-cor-lof-hetero.title: C2
exr-cor-lof-hetero.html: Suppose the groups have different variances σi2. Compute E(SSPE) and E(SSLF) under a correct mean model, and show by an example with two large groups of very different sizes and variances that the F test can then reject far more or far less often than α.

exr-cor-lof-power.title: C1
exr-cor-lof-power.html: A straight line is to be tested for lack of fit at the four values x=0,1,2,3, each replicated m times, when the true mean is β0+β1x+β2x2 with β2/σ=0.5. Show that γ=mβ22‖(I−M4)q‖2/σ2, where q=(0,1,4,9)⊤ and M4 is the projection for a line on the four points, and find the smallest m for which the test at level 0.05 has power at least 0.8.

exr-cor-lof-table.title: A1
exr-cor-lof-table.html: A straight line is fitted to n=24 observations at c=6 distinct values of x, each replicated four times. The residual sum of squares is 50.0 and the pure-error sum of squares is 36.0. Complete the analysis of variance table for lack of fit and compute F. Is there evidence of lack of fit at level 0.05, given that F0.05(4,18)=2.93?

exr-cor-lof-weighted.title: B1
exr-cor-lof-weighted.html: Show that the least squares estimate β^ from all n observations is also the weighted least squares estimate from the c group means, with weights ni, and that SSLF is the weighted residual sum of squares of that fit.

exr-cor-near-df.title: A1
exr-cor-near-df.html: A regression with an intercept and two regressors has n=30 cases, whose rows are grouped into 8 clusters of near replicates. Assuming no combination of cluster indicators lies in C(X) except the constant, give the degrees of freedom of the near-replicate test of X against [X,D].

exr-cor-nonnormal-r.title: B2
exr-cor-nonnormal-r.html: Let X and U be independent standard normal variables and Y=XU. Show that X and Y are uncorrelated but not independent, and that nr→N(0,3). What happens to the level of the test that rejects ρ=0 when |T|>tn−2,0.025 in large samples? Which assumption of @thm-cor-conditional fails?

exr-cor-omitted-prediction.title: C1
exr-cor-omitted-prediction.html: Let the rows (Xi⊤,Yi) be jointly normal with k regressors, and fit only the first k1<k of them. Show that the expected error on a new case is σ12(1+1/n)(n−2)/(n−k1−2), where σ12 is the error variance of the best linear predictor from the first k1 regressors. Hint: under joint normality the smaller model is itself a correct normal model with random regressors. For n=30, k=10, k1=4 and σ12=1.2σ2, is the smaller model better for prediction? What is the largest k1 for which it is?

exr-cor-optimism-numbers.title: A1
exr-cor-optimism-numbers.html: With normal regressors, n=50 and k=10, compute the expected in-sample error E(SSE/n) and the expected error on a new case, in units of σ2. By what factor does the first understate the second?

exr-cor-partial-df.title: A2
exr-cor-partial-df.html: Explain, in terms of dimensions of subspaces, why the t test of a partial correlation given q variables has n−q−2 degrees of freedom, and why this equals n−p for the corresponding regression.

exr-cor-partial-numbers.title: A1
exr-cor-partial-numbers.html: From n=40 cases, the partial correlation of y and x given q=3 other variables is −0.30. Compute the t statistic, its degrees of freedom, and the 95% Fisher interval for the population partial correlation.

exr-cor-partial-r2-beta.title: B1
exr-cor-partial-r2-beta.html: Let X=[X1,X2] with 1∈C(X1), rankX1=r1, rankX=r almost surely, and suppose that, given the regressors, Y follows the normal linear model with mean X1β1. Show that the partial R2 of @def-ss-partial-r2 has the Beta(r−r12,n−r2) distribution, whatever the distribution of the regressors.

exr-cor-partition-projection.title: B1
exr-cor-partition-projection.html: Let X=(X1X2) and Z=(X100X2). Show that C(X)⊆C(Z), that the projection onto C(Z) is (M100M2), and that SSE(Z) is the sum of the residual sums of squares of the two separate regressions.

exr-cor-r-general-variance.title: C1
exr-cor-r-general-variance.html: For a general pair (X,Y) with finite fourth moments, standardized to means 0 and variances 1, show that n(r−ρ) is asymptotically normal with variance (1+ρ22)EX2Y2+ρ24(EX4+EY4)−ρ(EX3Y+EXY3). Check that it reduces to (1−ρ2)2 under normality, and explain why no transformation of r stabilizes the variance across all distributions.

exr-cor-r2-ceiling.title: B2
exr-cor-r2-ceiling.html: Suppose 1∈C(X). Show that every model whose model matrix has the row structure of X has R2≤1−SSPE/SST, with equality for the cell-means model.

exr-cor-r2-consistent.title: B3
exr-cor-r2-consistent.html: Show that R2→ρY⋅X2 with probability one as n→∞, without assuming normality, provided the rows are independent and identically distributed with finite second moments and ΣXX positive definite.

exr-cor-r2-invariance.title: B2
exr-cor-r2-invariance.html: Show that R2 is unchanged if Y is replaced by aY+b with a≠0, or the regressors by B⊤X+c with B nonsingular. Show that ρY⋅X2 has the same invariance.

exr-cor-r2-inverse-correlation.title: B1
exr-cor-r2-inverse-correlation.html: Let R be the sample correlation matrix of (Y,X1,…,Xk), assumed nonsingular, and let rYY be the (1,1) entry of R−1. Show that R2=1−1/rYY, and that 1−R2=detR/detRXX, where RXX is the correlation matrix of the regressors.

exr-cor-r2-lrt.title: C1
exr-cor-r2-lrt.html: With normal rows, show that the likelihood ratio statistic for ρY⋅X2=0 against an unrestricted alternative is (1−R2)n/2, so the likelihood ratio test is the overall F test. Hint: under the null the covariance matrix is block diagonal; use the proof of @prp-cor-mvn-mle and @exr-cor-r2-inverse-correlation.

exr-cor-r2-to-f.title: A1
exr-cor-r2-to-f.html: A regression on k=3 random regressors from n=40 cases has R2=0.25. Compute the overall F statistic and its degrees of freedom. Under the null hypothesis ρ2=0, what are the mean and the distribution of R2?

exr-cor-rainbow-df.title: B2
exr-cor-rainbow-df.html: In the rainbow test, order the cases so that the central subset of size m comes first, and let its model matrix Xc have rank r. Show that Z=(Xc00In−m) has C(X)⊆C(Z), that SSE(Z) is the residual sum of squares of the central fit, and that the test has n−m and m−r degrees of freedom.

exr-cor-reset-cubic.title: B4
exr-cor-reset-cubic.html: With a single regressor and an intercept, show that if β^1≠0, then C([1,x,y^2,y^3])=C([1,x,x2,x3]), powers taken entry by entry. Conclude that RESET is then the F test of the cubic polynomial.

exr-cor-semipartial.title: B2
exr-cor-semipartial.html: The semipartial correlation of y and x given Z is the correlation between y itself and the residual x~=(I−MD)x. Show that its square equals Rfull2−Rreduced2, the increase in R2 when x is added to [1,Z]. How does it relate to the squared partial correlation?

exr-cor-slope-numbers.title: A1
exr-cor-slope-numbers.html: In the setting of @prp-cor-slope-unconditional take n=20, σ=2 and σX=1. Compute the unconditional variance of β^1 and compare it with σ2/E(Sxx). Which quantile would you use for a 95% interval for β1 computed from one sample?

exr-cor-tukey-nonadditivity.title: C1
exr-cor-tukey-nonadditivity.html: In a two-way layout with one observation per cell and the additive model E(yij)=μ+αi+βj, Tukey’s statistic tests the added regressor (α^iβ^j). Show that, after the additive model is projected out, this regressor spans the same space as the entrywise square of the fitted values, and deduce from @thm-cor-fitted-regressors that Tukey’s test has an exact F(1,(a−1)(b−1)−1) null distribution.

exr-cor-two-correlations.title: A2
exr-cor-two-correlations.html: Two independent samples give r1=0.45 with n1=60 and r2=0.20 with n2=80. Test ρ1=ρ2 at level 0.05.

exr-cor-unbiased-cov.title: B3
exr-cor-unbiased-cov.html: In the setting of @cor-cor-slope-covariance, let s2=SSE/(n−k−1) and let W be the centred cross-product matrix. Show that s2W−1, the usual estimate of the covariance of the slopes, is an unbiased estimator of their unconditional covariance σ2ΣXX−1/(n−k−2).

exr-cor-variance-stabilizing.title: B1
exr-cor-variance-stabilizing.html: Suppose n(Tn−θ)→N(0,s(θ)2) for every θ in an interval, with s positive and continuous. Show that if g′(θ)=1/s(θ), then n(g(Tn)−g(θ))→N(0,1). Solve g′(ρ)=1/(1−ρ2) and recover @eq-cor-fisher-z.

exr-cor-which-exact.title: A2
exr-cor-which-exact.html: Under @def-cor-random-regressors, which of the following hold unconditionally: (i) E(s2)=σ2; (ii) Cov(β^)=σ2(X⊤X)−1; (iii) (n−p)s2/σ2∼χ2(n−p), independent of X; (iv) the 95% confidence ellipsoid for β has coverage 0.95?

exr-cor-z-interval-numbers.title: A1
exr-cor-z-interval-numbers.html: A sample of n=28 pairs has r=0.62. Compute the 95% Fisher interval for ρ.

lem-cor-bivariate-moments.title: Fourth moments of a standard bivariate normal pair
lem-cor-bivariate-moments.title_html: Fourth moments of a standard bivariate normal pair
lem-cor-bivariate-moments.html: Let (X,Y) be bivariate normal with means 0, variances 1 and correlation ρ. Then EX4=3, EX3Y=3ρ and EX2Y2=1+2ρ2. Consequently the covariance matrix of (X2,Y2,XY) is Γ=(22ρ22ρ2ρ222ρ2ρ2ρ1+ρ2).

lem-cor-centred-wishart.title: Centred cross-products
lem-cor-centred-wishart.html: Let X1,…,Xn (n≥2) be independent Nk(μ,Σ) vectors with mean X¯, and let W=∑i(Xi−X¯)(Xi−X¯)⊤. Then W∼Wk(n−1,Σ), and W is independent of X¯.

lem-cor-conditioning.title: Pivots given the design
lem-cor-conditioning.html: Let S be a random vector and U any random element. Suppose there is a distribution Q such that, for almost every value u, the conditional distribution of S given U=u is Q. Then S∼Q, and S is independent of U.

lem-cor-inverse-chisq.title: Mean of an inverse chi-squared variable
lem-cor-inverse-chisq.title_html: Mean of an inverse chi-squared variable
lem-cor-inverse-chisq.html: If V∼χ2(ν) with ν>2, then E(1/V)=1/(ν−2), the fact used without proof for @eq-ss-f-mean. For ν≤2 the mean is infinite.

lem-cor-inverse-wishart.title: Mean of an inverse Wishart matrix
lem-cor-inverse-wishart.title_html: Mean of an inverse Wishart matrix
lem-cor-inverse-wishart.html: Let W∼Wk(m,Σ) with Σ positive definite and m≥k+2. Then W is nonsingular with probability one, and E(W−1)=Σ−1m−k−1.

lem-cor-row-structure.title: The largest model with the same replicates
lem-cor-row-structure.title_html: The largest model with the same replicates
lem-cor-row-structure.html:
1. C(X)⊆C(Z). More generally, every matrix W with n rows whose rows are constant within the groups satisfies C(W)⊆C(Z).

  2. MZy replaces each observation by its group mean y¯i, and My is constant within groups.

prp-cor-augmented-test.title: Testing against any larger model
prp-cor-augmented-test.html:
Let Y∼Nn(θ,σ2I), let X have rank r, and let Z be a fixed matrix, chosen without reference to Y, with C(X)⊆C(Z) and rank(Z)=s, r<s<n. Let M and MZ be the two projections and F=[SSE(X)−SSE(Z)]/(s−r)SSE(Z)/(n−s).

  1. If θ∈C(X), then F∼F(s−r,n−s).

  2. If θ∈C(Z), then F∼F(s−r,n−s,‖(I−M)θ‖2/σ2).

  3. In general F=U/(s−r)V/(n−s) with independent U∼χ2(s−r,γ1) and V∼χ2(n−s,γ2), where γ1=‖(MZ−M)θ‖2/σ2 and γ2=‖(I−MZ)θ‖2/σ2. For every c>0, Pr(F>c) is strictly increasing in γ1 and strictly decreasing in γ2.

prp-cor-best-predictor.title: The best predictor and the correlation ratio
prp-cor-best-predictor.title_html: The best predictor and the correlation ratio
prp-cor-best-predictor.html:
Let EY2<∞, Var(Y)>0, and m(X)=E(Y∣X).

  1. A predictor g(X) with Eg(X)2<∞ equals m(X) with probability one iff Eg(X)=EY and Cov(h(X),Y−g(X))=0 for every square-integrable h.

  2. For every such g with Varg(X)>0, corr(Y,g(X))2≤η2=Varm(X)VarY,{#eq-cor-correlation-ratio}

    with equality for g=m when Varm(X)>0. The correlation ratio η2 exceeds the squared multiple correlation ρY⋅X2 of @prp-rv-multiple-correlation by E(m(X)−L(Y∣X))2/VarY, so η2=ρY⋅X2 iff m is affine.

prp-cor-mvn-mle.title: Maximum likelihood with normal rows
prp-cor-mvn-mle.html: Suppose the sample covariance matrix of the rows is nonsingular. The maximum likelihood estimates of (α,β,σ2) are the least squares estimates and SSE/n, and the maximum likelihood estimate of ρY⋅X2 is R2.

prp-cor-optimism.title: In-sample and out-of-sample error
prp-cor-optimism.html:
1. (Fixed design.) Let E(Y)=Xβ and Cov(Y)=σ2In with rank(X)=r, and let Y∗ be a vector of new responses at the same design, uncorrelated with Y, with the same mean and covariance. Then E‖Y−Xβ^‖2n=σ2n−rn,E‖Y∗−Xβ^‖2n=σ2n+rn, so the in-sample error understates the error on new responses by 2rσ2/n on average.

  2. (Normal random design.) In the setting of @thm-cor-prediction-error, the in-sample error has E(SSE/n)=σ2(n−k−1)/n, and the error on a new case is @eq-cor-prediction-error.

prp-cor-partial-coefficient.title: Partial correlation and the regression coefficient
prp-cor-partial-coefficient.title_html: Partial correlation and the regression coefficient
prp-cor-partial-coefficient.html: Let (Y,X,Z) have finite second moments, with Cov((Z⊤,X)⊤) positive definite, and let βX be the coefficient of X in the best linear predictor of Y from (Z,X). Then βX=σyx⋅Zσxx⋅Z=ρyx⋅Zσyy⋅Zσxx⋅Z, so βX=0 iff ρyx⋅Z=0.

prp-cor-prediction-decomposition.title: Excess error of a fitted linear predictor
prp-cor-prediction-decomposition.title_html: Excess error of a fitted linear predictor
prp-cor-prediction-decomposition.html: Let (X0,Y0) have finite second moments, Cov(X0)=ΣXX, mean μX, and best linear predictor L0=α∗+β∗⊤X0 with error variance σ∗2=E(Y0−L0)2. Let Y^0=a+b⊤X0, where (a,b) depend only on training data independent of (X0,Y0). Then, given the training data, E[(Y0−Y^0)2|training data]=σ∗2+(α∗−a+(β∗−b)⊤μX)2+(β∗−b)⊤ΣXX(β∗−b).

prp-cor-r-exact.title: Exact law of the sample correlation
prp-cor-r-exact.title_html: Exact law of the sample correlation
prp-cor-r-exact.html:
Let T=rn−2/1−r2 and δ=ρ/1−ρ2.

  1. Given the X values, T∼t(n−2,δV), where V=∑i(Xi−X¯)2/σX2.

  2. V∼χ2(n−1), and for −1<c<1, Pr(r≤c)=E[Pr{t(n−2,δV)≤cn−2/1−c2}].{#eq-cor-r-cdf}

  3. If ρ=0, then T∼t(n−2) and r2∼Beta(12,n−22), independently of the X values.

  4. The law of r is stochastically increasing in ρ: for each c∈(−1,1), Pr(r≤c) is a strictly decreasing function of ρ.

prp-cor-slope-unconditional.title: The slope under a random normal regressor
prp-cor-slope-unconditional.title_html: The slope under a random normal regressor
prp-cor-slope-unconditional.html: Let (Xi,Yi), i=1,…,n with n≥3, be independent draws from a bivariate normal distribution with Var(Xi)=σX2, regression slope β1 and conditional variance σ2=Var(Yi∣Xi). Let β^1 be the least squares slope. Then σXn−1σ(β^1−β1) ∼ t(n−1), so β^1 has heavier tails than any normal distribution, and for n>3 Var(β^1)=σ2σX2(n−3).{#eq-cor-slope-variance}

prp-cor-smoother-null.title: The smoother statistic is pivotal
prp-cor-smoother-null.html: If Y∼Nn(Xβ,σ2I), the distribution of T in @eq-cor-smoother-statistic depends only on X and S, not on β or σ2. It equals the distribution of ‖S(I−M)u‖2/‖(I−M)u‖2 with u∼Nn(0,I).

thm-cor-blup.title: Best linear unbiased predictor
thm-cor-blup.html:
Let Y=Xβ+ε and y0=x0⊤β+e0, with E(ε)=0, E(e0)=0, Cov(ε)=σ2V for a known positive definite V, Cov(ε,e0)=σ2v0 and Var(e0)=σ2v00. Suppose x0∈C(X⊤). A predictor a⊤Y+a0 is unbiased if E(a⊤Y+a0−y0)=0 for every β. Among unbiased linear predictors, the mean squared error E(y0−a⊤Y−a0)2 is minimized by y^0=x0⊤β~+v0⊤V−1(Y−Xβ~),{#eq-cor-blup}

where β~ solves the generalized least squares equations X⊤V−1Xb=X⊤V−1Y. With c=x0−X⊤V−1v0, its mean squared error is σ2[v00−v0⊤V−1v0+c⊤(X⊤V−1X)−c].

thm-cor-conditional.title: Conditional inference is valid unconditionally
thm-cor-conditional.html:
Assume the model of @def-cor-random-regressors, with n>p. Let β^=(X⊤X)−1X⊤Y and s2=‖Y−Xβ^‖2/(n−p).

  1. For every fixed λ≠0, the statistic T=(λ⊤β^−λ⊤β)/(sλ⊤(X⊤X)−1λ) has the t(n−p) distribution and is independent of X.

  2. Let Λ be a fixed p×q matrix of rank q, let d∈Rq, and put F=(Λ⊤β^−d)⊤[Λ⊤(X⊤X)−1Λ]−1(Λ⊤β^−d)qs2. Given X, F∼F(q,n−p,γ(X)) with γ(X)=(Λ⊤β−d)⊤[Λ⊤(X⊤X)−1Λ]−1(Λ⊤β−d)σ2.{#eq-cor-random-noncentrality}

    If Λ⊤β=d, then F∼F(q,n−p) unconditionally, independently of X.

  3. A confidence set whose coverage probability given X equals 1−α for almost every X has unconditional coverage 1−α. A test whose rejection probability under the null hypothesis equals α given almost every X has unconditional size α.

  4. The unconditional power of the level-α test that rejects when F>Fα(q,n−p) is E[π(γ(X))], where π(γ)=Pr{F(q,n−p,γ)>Fα(q,n−p)}.

thm-cor-fisher-z.title: Fisher’s z transformation
thm-cor-fisher-z.html: As n→∞, n(r−ρ)→N(0,(1−ρ2)2)andn(z−ζ)→N(0,1) in distribution. The same limits hold with n−3 in place of n. The limiting variance of z does not depend on ρ: tanh−1 is a variance-stabilizing transformation for r.

thm-cor-fitted-regressors.title: Regressors that are functions of the fitted values
thm-cor-fitted-regressors.title_html: Regressors that are functions of the fitted values
thm-cor-fitted-regressors.html: Let Y∼Nn(Xβ,σ2I) with rank(X)=r. Let W=w(MY) be an n×q matrix computed from the fitted values alone, with rank[X,W]=r+q<n with probability one. Then F=[SSE(X)−SSE([X,W])]/qSSE([X,W])/(n−r−q) ∼ F(q,n−r−q).

thm-cor-lack-of-fit.title: Pure-error lack-of-fit test
thm-cor-lack-of-fit.html:
Let Y∼Nn(θ,σ2I) with θ∈C(Z), that is, E(yij)=μi depends only on the row of X; assume r<c<n. Then:

  1. SSE=SSLF+SSPE, and SSLF and SSPE are independent;

  2. SSPE/σ2∼χ2(n−c) for every μ1,…,μc;

  3. SSLF/σ2∼χ2(c−r,γ) with γ=‖(I−M)θ‖2σ2=1σ2∑i=1cni(μi−μ~i)2,{#eq-cor-lof-noncentrality}

    where μ~i is the ith group value of Mθ, the least squares fit to the true means;

  4. the ratio F=SSLF/(c−r)SSPE/(n−c)∼F(c−r,n−c,γ), and γ=0 iff θ∈C(X), that is, iff the model is correct. The test that rejects the model when F>Fα(c−r,n−c) has size α, and its power increases strictly with γ.

thm-cor-partial-law.title: Distribution of a sample partial correlation
thm-cor-partial-law.title_html: Distribution of a sample partial correlation
thm-cor-partial-law.html:
Let Z be a random n×q matrix with rank[1,Z]=q+1 with probability one, and n≥q+3. Suppose that, given Z, the rows (yi,xi) are independent bivariate normal vectors with means a+Bz(i), affine in the ith row z(i) of Z, and a common covariance matrix with correlation ρ. Then ryx⋅Z has the same distribution as the sample correlation of n−q independent bivariate normal pairs with correlation ρ, and it is independent of Z.

In particular, if the rows (yi,xi,z(i)⊤) are independent draws from a multivariate normal distribution with a nonsingular covariance matrix, the conclusion holds with ρ=ρyx⋅Z, the population partial correlation.

thm-cor-partial-test.title: The partial correlation test is the coefficient t test
thm-cor-partial-test.title_html: The partial correlation test is the coefficient t test
thm-cor-partial-test.html:
Regress y on the p=q+2 columns [1,Z,x], assumed of full rank, and let t be the t statistic of the coefficient of x for the value zero. Then:

  1. for every data set, t=n−pryx⋅Z/1−ryx⋅Z2;

  2. under the assumptions of @thm-cor-partial-law with ρ=0, t∼t(n−p), whatever the distribution of Z;

  3. when the rows are multivariate normal, the t test of the coefficient of x and the test of ρyx⋅Z=0 are the same test, and it has exact size.

thm-cor-prediction-error.title: Prediction error under normal regressors
thm-cor-prediction-error.html: In the setting of @cor-cor-slope-covariance, let (X0,Y0) be a further independent draw and Y^0=α^+β^⊤X0 the fitted predictor. If n≥k+3, then E(Y0−Y^0)2=σ2(1+1n)n−2n−k−2.{#eq-cor-prediction-error}

thm-cor-r2-distribution.title: Distribution of R^2 with normal rows
thm-cor-r2-distribution.title_html: Distribution of R2 with normal rows
thm-cor-r2-distribution.html:
Under the assumptions above, let F=n−k−1kR21−R2 and λ=ρ2/(1−ρ2).

  1. Given the regressors, F∼F(k,n−k−1,γ) with γ=β⊤Wβ/σ2, where W is the centred cross-product matrix of the regressors.

  2. If ρ2=0, then F∼F(k,n−k−1) and R2∼Beta(k2,n−k−12), independently of the regressors. The overall F test of the regression is an exact size-α test of ρ2=0, which under joint normality is the hypothesis that Y is independent of X.

  3. If ρ2>0, then γ=λV with V∼χ2(n−1), and for 0<c<1 Pr(R2≤c)=E[Pr{F(k,n−k−1,λV)≤(n−k−1)ck(1−c)}].{#eq-cor-r2-mixture}

  4. For each c∈(0,1), Pr(R2>c) is a strictly increasing function of ρ2∈[0,1).
